faq.a: In settings where imaging is unavailable, use WHO IMCI criteria (cough + fast breathing + chest indrawing) to start empiric antibiotics.
faq.q: Can I treat pneumonia without a chest X‑ray?

faq.a: Add a macrolide if atypical pathogens are likely (young adult, no comorbidities) or if the patient is severely ill and coverage for atypicals is desired.
faq.q: When should I add a macrolide?

faq.a: Steroids are not routine for community‑acquired pneumonia; consider only in refractory septic shock or specific indications like COPD exacerbation.
faq.q: What is the role of steroids?

exam: A 45‑year‑old HIV‑positive man presents with fever, cough and SpO₂ 88 %; what is the next immediate step — assess severity with CURB‑65 and start supplemental O₂ plus empiric ceftriaxone and azithromycin.
You have a patient with a new infiltrate but a normal white cell count; how do you confirm bacterial pneumonia — rely on clinical picture and imaging; consider sputum Gram stain if available.
Which feature distinguishes pneumonia from pulmonary TB on chest X‑ray — lobar consolidation with air‑bronchograms in pneumonia versus upper‑lobe cavitation in TB.
A patient fails to improve after 48 h of amoxicillin; what should you consider — possible resistant organism, atypical pathogen, or empyema; obtain sputum culture and repeat imaging.
Why is a fluoroquinolone avoided in a patient with known seizure disorder — risk of lowering seizure threshold; choose a beta‑lactam instead.
What vaccination strategy reduces future episodes in this population — give pneumococcal conjugate vaccine and annual influenza vaccine at discharge.
Explain why pulse oximetry is essential in low‑resource settings — it provides an objective measure of hypoxia guiding oxygen therapy when arterial blood gases are unavailable.
A child with malaria and cough has a normal chest X‑ray; could they still have pneumonia — yes, malaria can mask pneumonia; treat empirically if clinical suspicion is high.
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: An infection of the lung parenchyma acquired outside hospitals, common in East African low‑resource settings. Diagnosis relies on clinical features and chest imaging, with severity guiding management.

b: Cough with sputum or dry, fever ≥38 °C, pleuritic chest pain
New infiltrate on chest X‑ray or, if unavailable, bedside lung ultrasound showing consolidation
sections.p: Acute infection of the pulmonary alveoli and interstitium presenting with cough, fever and infiltrates on chest X‑ray. Diagnosis requires compatible history, physical exam and radiographic confirmation.

t.b: Confirms presence of infiltrate; distinguishes pneumonia from TB or heart failure
Assesses oxygenation; guides need for supplemental O₂
Leukocytosis supports bacterial cause; neutrophilia suggests typical bacteria

b: Score 0–1: low risk, treat as outpatient
Score 2: consider short admission
Score ≥3: admit, consider ICU
sections.p: Severity determines inpatient vs outpatient care. Use the CURB‑65 score (confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age ≥ 65).

t.b: Part of CURB‑65; >30 breaths/min indicates severe disease
Elevated ≥7 mmol/L adds a point; reflects dehydration or renal impairment

b: Streptococcus pneumoniae – most frequent typical bacterium
Haemophilus influenzae – especially in HIV‑positive patients
Mycobacterium tuberculosis – chronic presentation, consider if weight loss >4 weeks
Atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia) – milder, often in younger adults
Viral (influenza, RSV) – seasonal peaks, may coexist with bacteria
sections.p: In East Africa the common aetiologies differ from high‑income settings.

b: Fever with rigors, night sweats
Cough producing purulent sputum or dry cough
Dyspnoea, tachypnoea, use of accessory muscles
Crackles on auscultation, egophony over consolidation
sections.p: Typical presentation includes acute onset of fever, chills, productive cough and pleuritic chest pain. In low‑resource settings, co‑existing malaria or HIV may modify the picture.
Select tests that answer specific clinical questions; when a test is unavailable, rely on bedside assessment.

t.b: Identifies bacterial pathogen; guides targeted antibiotics
Detects immunosuppression that alters likely pathogens and prognosis
Excludes concurrent malaria, which can mimic fever and respiratory distress

b: SpO₂ < 90 % or PaO₂ < 60 mmHg
Confusion or altered mental status
Systolic BP < 90 mmHg or MAP < 65 mmHg
Multilobar involvement or empyema on imaging
sections.p: Identify patients at risk of rapid deterioration.

b: Empiric antibiotics: amoxicillin‑clavulanate or high‑dose amoxicillin for typical bacteria; add macrolide if atypical coverage needed
In HIV‑positive or severe disease, use ceftriaxone plus azithromycin
Supplemental O₂ to keep SpO₂ ≥ 94 % (≥ 90 % in COPD)
Hydration, antipyretics, analgesia
Avoid fluoroquinolones in patients with known QT prolongation or seizure risk
sections.p: Treat the causative organism promptly and provide supportive care.

b: If no improvement, reassess for resistant organisms, TB, or empyema
Pneumococcal vaccine (PCV13/23) and annual influenza vaccine
Smoking cessation counseling, improve indoor air quality
sections.p: Re‑evaluate clinical response within 48‑72 hours and vaccinate at discharge.

b: Pulmonary tuberculosis – chronic course, weight loss, night sweats, upper‑lobe cavitation
Pulmonary embolism – sudden pleuritic pain, tachycardia, clear lungs on X‑ray
Heart failure – bilateral crackles, peripheral oedema, cardiomegaly on X‑ray
sections.p: Conditions that share fever and respiratory symptoms.

b: Normal white cell count does not rule out bacterial pneumonia
Chest X‑ray may be normal early; repeat if suspicion persists
Sputum culture can be contaminated; interpret with clinical context
sections.p: Be aware of atypical presentations and test limitations.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe dyspnoea or inability to speak full sentences
